readMe: Every threshold the session decision engine applies lives here, with the
provenance of that threshold attached to it. The engine reads its numbers
from this file: editing a `value` here changes what the engine decides.
This file is data, not documentation of data.
The field that matters most is `basis`. It answers a question that a
citation list cannot: is this threshold a cut point on a quantity the
outside world defines, or a cut point on a score Evidra computes itself?
external_metric    The quantity is defined outside Evidra (an
acute:chronic ratio, days since the last session).
Literature can speak to it, so `sources` is required
and `contested` records published disagreement.
internal_composite The quantity is a score Evidra invents by weighting
signals together. No published study has ever used
this score, so no publication can support a cut point
on it. `sources` MUST be empty and `evidenceLevel`
MUST be internal_heuristic. This is enforced by
assertValidRuleLibrary, not by convention.
That invariant exists because the tempting failure here is to attach a
real paper to an invented number and call the rule evidence-based. A
reviewer who checks the citation would find it does not mention the score
the threshold sits on. An empty `sources` on an internal_composite rule is
the honest state, not an unfinished one.
Every citation also carries `verificationStatus`, which says how far anyone
here has actually read it. A citation is a claim about a document, and that
claim is checkable independently of whether the document supports our
threshold. The vocabulary, strongest first:
primary_full_text_verified          The quoted figures were read in the
primary text at the URL given.
abstract_verified_full_text_not_read
Bibliographic record and quoted
phrases confirmed against the
published abstract. The body is
obtainable but nobody has read it.
abstract_verified_full_text_paywalled
As above, and the body is behind a
paywall, so the gap will not close by
someone simply getting round to it.
numbers_from_secondary_sources      Figures came from summaries of the
paper, not the paper. Treat as
unconfirmed.
citation_not_read_in_full           Legacy of the above two; do not use
for new entries.
A status may only move up when someone reads further, and moves down the
moment a check fails. Rules whose provenance was corrected downward record
the correction in `notes` rather than quietly dropping the old claim.

categories.description: Recovery state, accumulated load and lost fitness.
Progression toward the athlete's stated goal.

arbitrationPolicy.description: Which rule the decision is attributed to. Rules sort by category rank ascending, then priority descending, then ruleId. The first is the governing rule.
arbitrationPolicy.note: Every rule in this library version is in the recovery category, so this policy does not yet arbitrate between categories. It is implemented now so that adding the first injury or illness rule does not also require inventing the ordering under time pressure.

combinationPolicy.description: How the effects of several triggered rules combine. Intensity reductions do not sum; the largest single reduction applies. Duration caps apply independently and the lowest cap wins.
combinationPolicy.note: Arbitration and combination are separate policies on purpose. The governing rule explains the decision; it does not necessarily set the size of the change.

rules.title: Very low readiness replaces the session with recovery

measuredQuantity.name: readiness score
measuredQuantity.definition: A recovery score (itself a weighted blend of sleep 0.35, HRV 0.35, resting heart rate 0.20, stress 0.10, with vendor composites weighted above raw signals) minus a workload penalty of (ACWR - 1.2) x 22 and a fatigue penalty of maxMuscleFatigue x 0.22.
measuredQuantity.whyNoSourceIsPossible: Every weight in that expression was chosen by us. No study has measured outcomes against this score, so no study can support a cut point on it.

limitations: 40 and 30 are our own choices. They have not been calibrated against any outcome data, and calibrating them against simulated physiological values is prohibited (that would be fitting the engine to invented people).

The recovery score falls back to a neutral 50 when no fresh recovery signal is present, so a total absence of evidence cannot trigger this rule. That is deliberate, and it is reported through signalCoverage.
rules.notes: The severity here is the reason the effect is a swap rather than a step down: one notch off a hard session still prescribes training load on a day the evidence says to take none.

rules.title: Low readiness pulls intensity down one step

supportingLiterature.citation: Javaloyes A, Sarabia JM, Lamberts RP, Moya-Ramon M, et al. Training prescription guided by heart rate variability vs. predefined training: systematic review and meta-analysis, 2019-2021.
supportingLiterature.supports: Varying daily prescription from a daily recovery measurement, rather than following a fixed plan, has been tested in randomised trials: small-to-medium benefit on submaximal parameters, and lower dispersion of outcomes.
supportingLiterature.doesNotSupport: Any numeric cut point, and specifically not 60 on Evidra's readiness score. These trials used HRV-derived indices, not this composite.
supportingLiterature.whyItIsHereAnyway: It supports the direction of the rule (adjust today from today's recovery reading) while explicitly not supporting its number. Recording that split is the point of this field.

limitations: 60 is our own choice.

This rule is skipped when the scheduled session is already low intensity, and when the caller states no intensity at all — in the second case the blocked rule is reported in `limits` rather than silently dropped.
rules.notes: supportingLiterature is deliberately a different field from sources. sources means 'this publication supports this threshold'. Nothing supports this threshold.

rules.title: A maxed-out muscle group takes no further stimulus today

measuredQuantity.name: per-muscle-group fatigue
measuredQuantity.definition: Sum over recent sessions of trainingLoad x decay, where decay = max(0.15, 1 - ageDays/5), attributed to the muscle groups the session targeted, clamped to 0-100.
measuredQuantity.whyNoSourceIsPossible: The decay curve, its floor, and the 0-100 clamp are ours. The resulting number is not a physiological measurement and no publication reports outcomes against it.

limitations: 90 is our own choice, and so are the decay constants that produce the number it is compared against.

A session carrying no training load contributes nothing to this sum. That is reported through signalCoverage.training.missing and is the only way a caller learns the fatigue figure is built on partial evidence.
rules.notes: Two steps rather than one: at the ceiling, a single notch still leaves the session loading the same tissue.

rules.title: High fatigue in the target muscle group rules out hard work on it

supportingLiterature.citation: American College of Sports Medicine. Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2009;41(3):687-708.
supportingLiterature.supports: That resistance training is prescribed at a per-week frequency that rises with training status, verbatim: "2-3 d x wk(-1) for novice training, 3-4 d x wk(-1) for intermediate training, and 4-5 d x wk(-1) for advanced training"; and that sessions are sequenced by muscle group, verbatim: "large before small muscle group exercises". A frequency ceiling of this kind presupposes that a loaded muscle group needs recovery before it is loaded hard again, which is the direction of this rule.
supportingLiterature.doesNotSupport: The value 65, the decay model that produces the score it is compared against, and the claim that recovery is tracked per muscle group rather than globally. The abstract prescribes whole-session weekly frequency, not a per-muscle-group recovery interval; our earlier wording asserted the latter and has been withdrawn.

verification.against: PubMed record 19204579. Title, journal, year, volume, issue and pages confirmed; the two quoted phrases are in the published abstract.
verification.outcome: The bibliographic record and both quotations are confirmed against the abstract. The full 22-page position stand was not read, so anything it says beyond the abstract remains unchecked.

supportingLiterature.whyItIsHereAnyway: It supports the existence of a recovery interval between hard sessions for the same tissue. It says nothing about our number.

limitations: 65 is our own choice.

Only the abstract of the supporting citation has been read (verificationStatus: abstract_verified_full_text_not_read). It must not be described as fully verified until someone reads the position stand itself.

The abstract's frequency guidance is per week and per athlete, not per muscle group. This rule's per-muscle-group granularity is finer than anything the citation establishes, and that gap is ours, not the literature's.
rules.notes: Provenance re-reviewed 2026-08-07: the previous `supports` line claimed the position stand established per-muscle-group rather than global progression management. That is not in the abstract and was withdrawn rather than left standing on a citation nobody had opened.

rules.title: Moderate fatigue is reported but changes nothing
limitations: 45 is our own choice.
rules.notes: An advisory rule. It is in the library rather than inline because a rule that deliberately changes nothing is still a rule the athlete is entitled to see, and because it also gates the progression rule EVD-R-008.

rules.title: An acute load spike pulls intensity down one step

measuredQuantity.name: acute:chronic workload ratio
measuredQuantity.definition: Sum of training load over the last 7 days, divided by max(sum over the last 28 days / 4, weeklyTrainingLoadTarget).

sources.citation: Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med. 2016;50(5):273-280.
sources.supports: That acute (1 week) to chronic (rolling 4-week) load ratio is associated with injury risk. Verbatim from the paper: a ratio "within the range of 0.8-1.3 could be considered the training 'sweet spot'"; ratios ">=1.5 represent the 'danger zone'"; and at >=1.5 "the risk of injury was 2-4 times greater in the subsequent 7 days".

verification.against: Open-access full text at PMC4789704, confirmed by its own record to be Br J Sports Med 2016;50(5):273-280, doi 10.1136/bjsports-2015-095788.
verification.outcome: The 0.8-1.3 band and the 1.5 spike are present in the primary text as the quotations above. They were previously carried from secondary summaries; that caveat is retired.

contested.citation: Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ. Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020.
contested.objection: Mathematical coupling (acute load appears in both numerator and denominator); no coherent causal interpretation; adds no predictive value over acute load alone.

contested.citation: Lolli L, Batterham AM, Hawkins R, et al. Br J Sports Med, 2017-2019.
contested.objection: Ratio indices invite spurious correlation and inflated odds ratios; the published 'sweet spot' figure is argued to be an artefact.

limitations: 1.4 matches neither published figure: it sits between the band ceiling (1.3) and the spike definition (1.5). It is our choice, not the literature's.

When observed chronic load falls below weeklyTrainingLoadTarget the denominator becomes that target, so the ratio compares acute load against a goal rather than against this athlete's own chronic load. Reported as chronicBasis: baseline_floor.
weeklyTrainingLoadTarget (360) is itself unsourced, so the baseline_floor state inherits an unsourced denominator.
Given the objections above, read this as a ramp-rate guard, not injury prediction. That is why the effect is one step down and not a stop.
rules.notes: The only rule here whose quantity is externally defined and externally studied, and therefore the only one carrying a contested list. Citing Gabbett without citing Impellizzeri would misrepresent the state of the field, so both travel together. On verification (2026-08-07): the earlier publisher PDF was not machine-readable, so the figures had been taken from secondary summaries; the open-access deposit at PMC4789704 is readable and both figures are confirmed verbatim in the primary text. The contested entries below are still unread in full and are recorded from their published objections, not from our reading of them. Sessions carrying no training load are excluded from both sums.

rules.title: The first session back after a break is scaled down

measuredQuantity.name: days since last session, and percentage loss of chronic training load from its recent peak
measuredQuantity.definition: Detraining is flagged only when both an idle-days condition and a CTL-loss condition hold, measured against this athlete's own recent CTL peak.

effect.intensityStepsDown: 1, or 2 when either severe threshold is met

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med. 2000;30(2):79-87.
sources.supports: That a break under 4 weeks already costs aerobic capacity. Verbatim: "a rapid decline in maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) and blood volume", and "Ventilatory efficiency and endurance performance are also impaired."
sources.doesNotSupport: Any percentage, any number of days, and the values 42, 60 and 0.6. The abstract gives no figures at all; "rapid" is the whole of its quantification.

verification.against: PubMed record 10966148. Title, journal, year, volume, issue and pages confirmed; both quotations are in the published abstract. Full text is behind the publisher paywall and was not obtained.
verification.outcome: Direction confirmed, magnitude not. The figure "roughly 4-7% VO2max within 2-3 weeks" that this source previously carried is not in the abstract of either part and could not be traced to the primary text; it has been removed rather than restated.

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part II: long term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med. 2000;30(3):145-154.
sources.supports: That the loss keeps growing past 4 weeks and recent gains go first. Verbatim: "declines markedly but remains above control values during long term detraining, whereas recently acquired VO2max gains are completely lost." That scaling is why this rule has a severe tier.
sources.doesNotSupport: Any percentage or cut point. "Markedly" is the strongest quantitative word in the abstract.

verification.against: PubMed record 10999420. Title, journal, year, volume, issue and pages confirmed; the quotation is in the published abstract. Full text is behind the publisher paywall and was not obtained.
verification.outcome: The monotonic direction is confirmed from the primary abstract. Nothing numeric is.

limitations: 42, 60 and 0.6 are our own choices. The sources support the direction only; neither abstract contains a single number, so there is nothing in them for these cut points to be near or far from.
The detraining literature measures VO2max. Our trigger measures modelled chronic training load — a proxy for training done, not for fitness retained.
0.6 sits inside the common 'half to two-thirds of prior volume' return guidance, which is practitioner convention rather than a trial result.
Both sources are narrative reviews read at abstract level only, which is why evidenceLevel is expert_consensus and not systematic_review.
rules.notes: This rule exists because no recovery signal can see it. An athlete two months off reads rested: readiness high, muscle fatigue near zero, and ACWR at 0 — the safest possible value to EVD-R-006. Every other guard passes. Lost fitness therefore needs its own trigger rather than being inferred from recovery. Provenance re-reviewed 2026-08-07: this rule previously claimed "roughly 4-7% VO2max within 2-3 weeks, substantially more beyond 4 weeks" and an evidenceLevel of systematic_review. Neither survived the check — the percentages are in neither abstract, the full texts are paywalled, and both papers are narrative reviews by two authors with no systematic search method described. Both claims were corrected downward. This library's vocabulary has no narrative_review level, so expert_consensus is the nearest honest rung; adding one is a schema change, not something to fake with the levels available. Retracting a claim is the expected outcome of a provenance review, not a failure of one.

rules.title: High readiness with a fresh target muscle group allows a step up
limitations: 85 and 45 are our own choices.
A detrained athlete reads fresh on both quantities. This rule must therefore never fire while EVD-R-007 is active, and that exclusion is part of the rule, not an implementation detail.
rules.notes: The only rule in this library outside the recovery category. It is what makes the arbitration policy observable today: when it and a recovery rule both trigger, category rank decides which rule the decision is attributed to.
